content: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis and Yersinia enterocolitica 1. Enterocolitis Treatment: Early antimicrobial therapy has not been shown to reduce the frequency or severity of chronic sequelae in infections caused by Yersinia enterocolitica or Yersinia pseudotuberculosis. These organisms are susceptible to ampicillin, third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, and chloramphenicol. 2. Septicemia Treatment: The preferred regimen is ceftriaxone 1 g administered intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV) every 12 hours. For pediatric patients, the dose is ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day (up to 2 g/day) IM or IV every 12 hours. While no definitive treatment duration has been established, infections with Yersinia species are often treated for at least three weeks. Yersinia pestis (Plague) 1. Preferred Treatment: Streptomycin at 15 mg/kg/day. 2. Alternative Regimens: Chloramphenicol 50 mg/kg/day IV or orally (PO) every 6 hours for 10 days. Tetracycline 2 g/day PO in four divided doses for 10 days. Pediatric dosing involves a loading dose of 15 mg/kg followed by 25–50 mg/kg/day (up to 2 g/day) PO in four divided doses for 10 days. Sulfadiazine with a loading dose of 2–4 g, then 1 g PO every 4–6 hours. Doxycycline 200 mg/day PO every 12–24 hours. 3. Notes: Fluoroquinolones have demonstrated efficacy against Y. pestis in vitro and in animal studies, but no human studies have been published. Other antibiotics have been shown to be ineffective against plague. Neutropenic Fever 1. Preferred Regimens: Monotherapy options include piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem, meropenem, cefepime, or ceftazidime. For penicillin-allergic patients, ciprofloxacin plus clindamycin or aztreonam plus vancomycin may be used. 2. Notes: Monotherapy is generally preferred as no studies have shown combination therapy to be superior. Vancomycin should be added if there are signs of severe sepsis, hemodynamic instability, pneumonia, or suspected catheter-related infections. Empiric antifungal coverage should be considered in high-risk patients with persistent fever after 4–7 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics. MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome) Treatment: Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment. Notes: Experimental therapies such as interferons, ribavirin, lopinavir, and others are under investigation but not currently recommended. Supportive care includes oxygen administration for respiratory distress, conservative fluid management, and early recognition and treatment of sepsis. Penicilliosis 1. Mild Disease: Itraconazole 200 mg PO twice daily for 8–12 weeks. 2. Moderate to Severe Disease: Liposomal amphotericin B (3–5 mg/kg/day IV) or amphotericin B lipid complex (5 mg/kg/day IV) for 2 weeks, followed by itraconazole 200 mg PO twice daily for 10 weeks. 3. Maintenance Therapy: Itraconazole 200 mg PO daily. 4. Notes: Serum levels of itraconazole and voriconazole should be monitored to ensure adequate absorption. Mucormycosis Treatment: Surgical debridement of affected tissues combined with antifungal therapy. Liposomal amphotericin B (5–10 mg/kg/day IV) is the preferred antifungal agent. Alternative options include posaconazole or isavuconazole. Notes: Growth factors and granulocyte transfusions may be used to aid recovery from neutropenia. Correct metabolic acidosis and hyperglycemia as part of supportive care. Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) and HHV-7 1. HHV-6: Supportive therapy is the mainstay of treatment. In immunocompromised patients, consider ganciclovir, acyclovir, foscarnet, or cidofovir, although no antiviral regimens are validated by clinical trials. 2. HHV-7 (Roseola): Supportive therapy is sufficient for immunocompetent hosts with uncomplicated skin manifestations. In HIV-positive patients, antiretroviral therapy may be advisable. Cidofovir and foscarnet are the most active antiviral agents against HHV-7. Hepatitis E Treatment: Supportive care is the primary approach. Notes: Hepatitis E is usually self-limiting, and hospitalization is rarely required except in cases of fulminant hepatitis or symptomatic pregnant women. Ebola Virus Treatment: Supportive care is critical as no specific antiviral therapy is available. Supportive Measures: Isolate the patient. Administer IV fluids and maintain electrolyte balance. Provide oxygen and blood products as needed. Treat co-infections and manage complications such as renal failure or severe diarrhea. Notes: Recovery depends on supportive care and the patient’s immune response. Convalescent plasma has shown promise in some cases. Long-term complications, such as joint and vision problems, may occur in survivors.
